blocks.body_html:
Open technologies are transforming how organizations source, build, and innovate. Understanding how to procure and work with these technologies is now a critical skill for modern procurement and project leaders.

In this module, you'll explore:

items_html: What open technologies are and why “open” is about freedom to use, modify, and share – not just about cost.
The benefits of open technologies for procurement, cost optimization, risk reduction, and innovation.
How to qualify open technology ecosystems to ensure suppliers, components, and communities meet your organization’s needs.
Open-source commercial models and approaches to project execution for OCP-based and open-source solutions.
The Open Technology Game, including the five levels of engagement that help organizations leverage open technologies strategically.

blocks.body_html:
By the end of this module, you’ll have the insight and tools to make informed procurement decisions, collaborate with open technology ecosystems, and unlock the full value of OCP-based and open-source products.

Get ready to transform the way your organization sources, builds, and innovates with open technologies!

Let's get started by looking at what open technologies are.

blocks.heading_html: What are Open Technologies?

blocks.body_html:
When we talk about open technologies, you might think of something that’s free, or costs nothing.

That’s one of the biggest misconceptions.

In this context, “Open” doesn’t mean free as in price. It means free as in freedom – freedom to use, study, modify, and share. Think “freedom of speech” rather than “free beer”.

This simple shift in thinking has quietly shaped much of the digital world we live in today – from the phones in our pockets to the cloud services that power businesses.

blocks.complete_hint: Complete the content above before moving on.

blocks.heading_html: Types of Open Technologies
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

The principles of open technology started with just software, but they’ve spread far beyond that over the past few decades. Today, open technologies fit into four main categories.

Click each flipcard to learn more.

front.description_html: Open Software

back.description_html: Software where the source code is public. Anyone can look at it, tweak it, and share improvements. The Open Source Initiative defines principles, but the idea is simple: transparency, collaboration, and freedom to innovate.

Hardware designs, schematics, and blueprints shared publicly. Defined by the Open Source Hardware Association, this allows people to understand how devices work, build their own versions, or even sell them.

Non-personal data made accessible to everyone. The Open Data Institute emphasizes that this helps researchers, small businesses, and citizens generate insights, develop tools, and improve communities.
Public specifications for systems, protocols, or formats developed through consensus. Open standards ensure that different systems can work together and remain compatible over time.

blocks.complete_hint: Complete the content above before moving on.

blocks.heading_html: Open-Source Licenses
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Open technologies give you freedom, but each comes with a license. Think of a license as a guidebook: it explains what you're allowed to do and what you need to respect.

For procurement professionals, understanding licenses is critical for different reasons:

items_html: Compliance: It ensures legal use and avoids intellectual property infringements.
Risk Management: It identifies potentially restrictive clauses that are essential to protecting the interests of a company.

blocks.body_html:
There are three types of licenses.

Click each tab to learn more.

items.description_html:
Copyleft Licenses with a Contaminating Effect

These licenses require that any software which incorporates or links to the open source code must be distributed under the same license terms. This condition “spreads” to proprietary components, which is known as a contaminating effect in software licensing terms.

Companies who develop proprietary solutions tend to avoid using software with this license.

Examples: GPLv2, GPLv3 and AGPLv3.

Copyleft Licenses without a Contaminating Effect

These licenses require that any modifications to the original open source code should be redistributed under the same license. However, they allow integration with proprietary components as long as the interface is clear and respected.

Examples: LGPLv2.1, EPLv1.0 and MPLv1.1.

Permissive Licenses

Permissive licenses allow users to modify, redistribute, and incorporate code into proprietary software without the obligation to release the modified source code. As long as basic attribution and license terms are respected, companies can commercialize derived works without sharing the source code.

Permissive licenses are widely adopted in commercial settings as they enable innovation without legal risk of source code disclosure.

Examples: MIT License Apache v2.0 or BSD.

blocks.label: CONTINUE
blocks.complete_hint: Complete the content above before moving on.

blocks.body_html:
Some companies also establish a list of licenses they accept or not. For instance, the buy me a beer license is often not accepted in large corporations.

This license grants users the freedom to use, modify, and redistribute software on the condition that, if the code proves useful, they might consider buying the author a beer as a token of appreciation.

It also reflects an informal, community-oriented spirit emblematic of early open-source culture. However, corporate legal teams and larger enterprises tend to reject it due to its lack of legal protection and enforceability.

blocks.heading_html: The History of Open Technologies
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Open technologies didn’t just appear overnight – they’ve grown and evolved over decades of collaboration. From early academic sharing to today’s digital backbone, the journey of open technologies is full of milestones, debates, and breakthroughs.

Let’s take a closer look at the history of open technologies.

2000s Going Mainstream Projects like Linux and Apache showed that open source could outperform proprietary software. Companies like IBM and Intel invested heavily, while tools like Git and GitHub made global collaboration seamless for both experts and newcomers. 1990s Switch to Open Source By the late 1990s, the term “free software” felt too political and risky for business. Christine Peterson suggested “open source,” and the Open Source Initiative (OSI) was founded in 1998. This new framing emphasized collaboration, reliability, and cost savings – making openness more appealing to the corporate world. 1970s – 1980s The Early Days Open technologies began in academic and hacker communities. Richard Stallman’s GNU Project and the Free Software movement championed software freedom and introduced copyleft licenses, ensuring code remained open for everyone. Present Open Everywhere Today, open technologies power the backbone of the digital world – from cloud infrastructure to AI frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch. Tech giants like Google, Meta, and Microsoft actively contribute, while entire industries rely on open standards, open data, and open hardware.

Openness has become not just a philosophy, but a foundation of modern innovation. The principles of openness and collaboration will continue shaping digital infrastructure, balancing ideals with real-world pragmatism.

blocks.body_html:
Open technologies provide real, structural advantages for organizations navigating digital transformation. From lowering costs to driving innovation, they’ve become powerful levers for procurement and strategy.

In this lesson, we’ll cover five key benefits of open technologies:

items_html: They form the foundation of digital infrastructure.
They deliver cost advantages across the full lifecycle.
They reduce dependency risks linked to single suppliers.
They help organizations standardise and simplify.
They accelerate innovation in ways closed systems can’t.

blocks.heading_html: The Foundation of Digital Infrastructure
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

What started as a small community movement has become the backbone of today’s digital economy. Open technologies are woven into nearly every system we rely on, from cloud infrastructure to artificial intelligence.

Why is this the case?

Click the plus icons to learn more.

items.title: Tackling Complexity
items.description_html: Today’s digital systems combine countless components, programming languages, and services. Open technologies provide high-quality, reusable parts and connectors that make it easier to integrate everything and to solve tough problems from multiple perspectives.

items.title: Flexibility and Customization
items.description_html: Unlike proprietary solutions, open technologies don’t force you to accept “one-size-fits-all”. Companies can adapt, extend, and fine-tune them to meet their exact business goals.

items.title: Faster Innovation
items.description_html: Open development is distributed and collaborative. Bugs get fixed quickly, new features roll out faster, and organizations can experiment and prototype without starting from scratch.

items.title: Avoiding Dependencies
items.description_html: With open technologies, you’re never locked into a single vendor for upgrades, support, or development. Instead, you can choose from multiple providers or your own in-house team, reducing both costs and risks.

items.title: Transparency and Auditability
items.description_html: Security and compliance are essential in the modern world. With open source, the code is fully visible, allowing independent audits, faster detection of vulnerabilities, and stronger trust in the system’s inner workings.

items.title: Collaboration at Scale
items.description_html: Perhaps the biggest strength: open technologies bring together a global community of developers, researchers, and businesses. This collective intelligence accelerates learning, sparks innovation, and ensures tools evolve to meet real-world needs.

blocks.body_html: Open technologies aren’t “alternative” solutions anymore. They are the invisible scaffolding of modern infrastructure that make our systems more adaptable, reliable, and innovative.

blocks.heading_html: Cost Advantages
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

For procurement teams, costs are always a balancing act between short-term price and long-term value. Open technologies shift that balance by reducing expenses across the entire lifecycle of a system.

Let's take a look at five substantial cost advantages.

Acquisition Cost Proprietary software often requires steep licensing fees. Open technologies eliminate this, giving immediate savings at adoption. Customization & Integration Cost Open source software offers full access to source code, enabling deeper and more cost-effective customization than proprietary software. Deployment Cost Open source software offer flexibility and can be deployed on-premises, on the cloud, or on a hybrid infrastructure which reduces constraints imposed by suppliers and the associated costs. Maintenance & Support Cost For open source software diverse options can be contracted for maintenance and support enabling flexible, usage-aligned spending in comparison to proprietary solutions. Exit & Migration Cost Open source offer easier and cost effective migration than proprietary solutions. 1 2 3 4 5
While proprietary software may offer speed and ease of deployment in the short term, open source software tends to deliver savings over the full lifecycle.
Harvard Business School researchers estimate that without open source, companies would spend 3.5× more on software than they do today. Source: Harvard Business School

Open hardware designs, such as those by OCP, also offer cost optimization opportunities.

This collaborative design approach helps to:

items_html: Reduce proprietary overheads.
Create parts and components that are optimized for essential functions only.
Develop a lean, cost-effective infrastructure.

blocks.body_html:
Companies further benefit from lower maintenance and upgrade costs if they have the right internal capabilities or if they use experienced integrators. For OCP, energy efficiencies can also be secured thanks to effective designs.

As a result, Yahoo Japan reported in 2019:
35% price advantage on servers 41% savings on racks by transitioning to OCP-based systems

These are not marginal gains – they are strategic levers for digital infrastructure cost control.

Source: European Business Review

blocks.heading_html: Reducing Dependency Risks
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

One of procurement’s constant challenges is managing risk. Relying too heavily on a single vendor can mean higher costs, reduced flexibility, or even operational vulnerability if that supplier exits the market. Open technologies offer clear solutions to mitigate this dependency.

Click each flipcard to learn more.

back.description_html: Because open technologies are shared, different vendors can compete to provide support, integration, and maintenance.

front.description_html: Healthy Ecosystems

back.description_html: Active open communities keep technologies alive and evolving, independent of any one company’s business decisions.

front.description_html: Hardware Freedom

back.description_html: With open designs, interoperable components can be sourced from different manufacturers, reducing downtime and switching costs.

blocks.body_html: Open technologies help to replace dependence on a single vendor with the resilience of an ecosystem. For procurement, that means better negotiating power and lower supplier risk.

blocks.heading_html: Standardization
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Standardization is often misunderstood as the antithesis of innovation. This might be true for very basic product that turn into commodities when they are standardized but for more complex systems, the design behind standards can still evolve and improve.

Open technologies enable a powerful form of consensus-driven standardization that enhances compatibility while offering opportunities for further innovation. While the interoperability is maximized; the design of the software or hardware component is not fixed and can be innovated over time.

blocks.heading_html: Facilitating Innovation
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Perhaps the most profound benefit of open technologies is their effect on innovation. By opening the design process, sharing knowledge, and enabling collective development, open technologies accelerate discovery and shorten development cycles. They can also help create more sustainable solutions.

In the case of OCP, several innovation pathways have emerged along these lines:

Pathway

Description

Rapid iteration

When designs are shared openly, others can build upon them, refine them, and redeploy them without starting from scratch.

Circular economy models

Facebook and others resell wiped, refurbished hardware components to other companies, prolonging the lifecycle of equipment and reducing environmental impact.

Advanced cooling and energy reuse

Open collaboration channels focus attention on frontier sustainability issues like Advanced Cooling Solutions (ACS), now a core domain of innovation in OCP.
As a result, Facebook reported in 2018:
This is the same as removing 95,000 cars from the road for a year. 400,000 metric tons of carbon were saved

This mode of innovation is inclusive as it invites participation from start-ups, universities, and public actors who may not have the capital to compete in closed markets. The barriers to entry are lowered, and the possibilities for co-creation greatly expanded.

As a conclusion, the advantages of open technologies represent structural benefits that support competitive, resilient, and sustainable business strategies. For organizations navigating digital transformation, open technologies should be considered as pillars for the future.

blocks.body_html:
When procurement professionals think about qualification, the instinct is to look at a supplier: its financial health, its delivery track record, its compliance. But with open technologies, the story changes.

You’re not just qualifying one supplier, you’re qualifying an ecosystem. A network of contributors, tools, and organizations that collectively create, maintain, and evolve a technology.

That requires a new lens. Instead of only asking “Is this company reliable?”, you’re asking “Is this ecosystem fit for purpose?”

To help answer that question, we’ll walk through seven critical criteria. Each one highlights both the opportunities and the risks of working with open technologies. As you go, keep in mind: there’s no “one-size-fits-all”. The weight you give each factor depends on your project, your organizational constraints, and your long-term goals.

Click the carousel arrows to learn more.

items.title: Total Cost Optimization
items.description_html:
What it means

With open technologies, the cost picture is bigger than just “what’s the price tag?” Total cost includes design, integration, lifecycle maintenance, and the hidden costs of lock-in. Open ecosystems often reduce these by eliminating licence fees, encouraging reuse, and giving access to multiple suppliers.

Why it matters

Procurement isn’t only about saving money upfront – it’s about controlling costs over time. By tapping into shared resources and diverse suppliers, organizations can avoid dominant vendor mark-ups and spread costs across the lifecycle.

What to check

  1. Is the licensing fees eliminated or reduced?
  2. Does the ecosystem provide connectors and tools that can help with integrations and customization of open source software?
  3. Are there competitive solutions available at each stage of the lifecycle of the technology?
  4. How does cost vary across high- and low-volume product lines for open hardware?
  5. Can you re-use open hardware components
  6. Can we estimate savings along the full life cycle? With what precisions?

items.title: Design Flexibility and Speed
items.description_html:
What it means

Open ecosystems remove many barriers that slow down development – no long NDAs, no complex IP agreements. Teams can use community-shared tools, pre-built modules, and design kits to build and iterate faster.

Why it matters

In many industries, speed is strategic. Being able to customize or prototype quickly can make the difference between leading the market or lagging behind.

What to check

  1. Can we rapidly customize the technology?
  2. Are pre-validated building blocks available?
  3. Is the ecosystem responsive to our development pace?
  4. Can ecosystem members collaborate without legal complexity?
  5. Are suppliers or partners able to collaborate without long negotiation cycles?
  6. Where and when speed can be gained?
  7. Where and when the project be slowed down?

items.title: Stability and Modularity
items.description_html:
What it means

For open technologies to be reliable, they must be robust, stable, and modular. Stability means a strong core that evolves without breaking. Modularity means you can add, swap, or extend features without destabilizing the system.

Why it matters

Procurement doesn’t just buy innovation – it buys reliability. A modular and stable ecosystem allows teams to adapt systems to their needs while maintaining overall integrity.

What to check

  1. Are core components frozen or standardized?
  2. Is there a good balance between upgrades and stability?
  3. Can you easily select and implement some of the features and extensions?
  4. Can modules be safely extended and interfaced?
  5. Are testing and verification tools available?

items.title: White Box Transparency
items.description_html:
What it means

Unlike “black box” solutions, open ecosystems let you look under the hood. You can access source code or design files, trace dependencies, and verify components without relying solely on the vendor.

Why it matters

Transparency builds trust. It helps with safety, cyber security, compliance, and IP clarity – critical issues in regulated or high-risk industries.

What to check

  1. Is source code accessible for all ecosystem members?
  2. Can internal teams and external partners inspect it?
  3. Are there any technical dependencies?
  4. Is the ecosystem aligned with certification or regulatory standards?
  5. Is there clarity on IP ownership and usage rights?

items.title: Supplier Flexibility
items.description_html:
What it means

An open ecosystem isn’t tied to one vendor. It allows organizations to choose between multiple suppliers, pursue dual sourcing, or even localize supply when needed.

Why it matters

Supplier flexibility reduces risks of cost hikes, service discontinuity, or geopolitical disruption. It strengthens resilience by avoiding dependency on a single dominant player.

What to check

  1. Can you choose solutions from multiple suppliers?
  2. Can you switch or dual-source suppliers without redesign?
  3. Can you localize or regionalize supply?

items.title: Permissive Licensing
items.description_html:
What it means

Permissive licenses allow organizations to use, adapt, and commercialize technology without being forced to share proprietary modifications. They reduce legal risks and encourage adoption, though they can also lower the pressure for contributors to “give back”.

Why it matters

Clear, business-friendly licensing makes it easier for procurement to approve and integrate open technologies. It supports both innovation and commercialization strategies.

What to check

  1. Does the licence support proprietary use?
  2. Are there risks of licence contamination?
  3. Are governance mechanisms in place to encourage reciprocity?
  4. Are legal terms easy to interpret and enforce?

items.title: Growing and Active Ecosystem
items.description_html:
What it means

An open technology lives or dies by its community. A growing and active ecosystem includes users, developers, companies, and institutions who contribute tools, documentation, and governance.

Why it matters

Activity signals sustainability. A growing, engaged community means more support, faster innovation, and lower risks of abandonment.

What to check

  1. Is the number of ecosystem members growing?
  2. Is the ecosystem expanding across sectors and geographies?
  3. Are individuals, companies and institutions contributing back?
  4. Is governance transparent and inclusive?

blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

These seven criteria are not independent. Some, like licensing, stability, and ecosystem activity, form the foundation. Others, like cost savings or flexibility, are outcomes. A strong open ecosystem builds upon:

items_html: Stable and modular technology.
A legally safe and permissive license.
A dynamic community of developers and adopters.

blocks.body_html:
Together, these enable transparent, efficient, and adaptable sourcing strategies.

Adopting open technology is not just a technical decision. It is a strategic choice. The right ecosystem will support your organization's autonomy, agility, and long-term competitiveness. But careful qualification is essential. Use these seven criteria mentioned above as your compass.

The successful integration of open technologies into an organization’s projects requires a structured approach. By systematically addressing key questions underpinning project requirements, the execution models, and the supplier business models, an organization can maximize the benefits of Open technologies while mitigating risks.

The following questions force teams to confront trade-offs from the early phase of a project:

blocks.heading_html: Establishing an Execution Model
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Building on the analysis above, an execution model can be defined. It describes what is done in-house and what is outsourced.

One of the most critical decisions in project execution is selecting the right execution model. Below is a comparison of three approaches: in-house development, external suppliers, and hybrid models with their trade-offs.

Click each tab to learn more.

items.title: In-House Development
items.description_html:
Definition: Fully internal execution using the organization’s own team and resources.

Advantages:

  • Full Control: Direct oversight of priorities, timelines, and intellectual property (IP).

  • Differentiation: Ideal for projects requiring unique proprietary layers (e.g., customizing an open-source core for competitive advantage).

  • Long-Term Alignment: Ensures continuity with the company’s technical roadmap and culture.

Challenges:

  • Resource Intensity: Demands significant investment in hiring, training, and infrastructure.

  • Skill Gaps: Limited access to niche expertise

  • Slower Time-to-Market: May lag behind vendor-supported solutions in early phases.

items.title: External Suppliers
items.description_html:
Definition: Outsourcing the project to third-party experts.

Advantages:

  • Expertise on Demand: Immediate access to specialized skills.

  • Faster Deployment: Leverages pre-existing vendor tools and workflows.

  • Risk Mitigation: Shifts accountability for performance or compliance to the vendor.

Challenges:

  • Reduced flexibility: Dependency on proprietary tools or services may limit flexibility.

  • Costs: Premium pricing for support and custom work.

  • Alignment Risks: Vendor priorities may not fully match organizational goals.

items.title: Hybrid Model
items.description_html:
Definition: Combining in-house teams with external partners for specific phases or components.

Advantages:

  • Cost Efficiency: Outsources discrete tasks while retaining core control.

  • Flexibility: Balances speed (vendor support) with long-term ownership (in-house maintenance).

  • Knowledge Transfer: Vendors upskill internal teams during collaboration.

Challenges:

  • Coordination Overhead: Requires rigorous contract management and clear role definitions.

  • Transition Risks: Handoffs between vendors and internal teams can introduce delays.

blocks.heading_html: Open Technology Business Models
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

For companies evaluating open technologies, understanding the available business models on the market is crucial for making informed decisions. Each model offers specific benefits and risks, depending on a company’s priorities—whether cost, control, scalability, or vendor independence.

The challenge is always to get the best external support while minimizing dependencies?

Let's explore three common business models and their implications for buyers.

Click each tab to learn more.

items.description_html:
Open-Core Model

In the open-core model, the basic building blocks of the technology are open and freely available, while advanced features, such as enterprise-grade security, scalability, or management tools, are proprietary and monetized. We see this model as a classic open Hardware model where a specialist manufacturer provides the hardware.

This is a cost effective starting point for some projects that are likely to scale over time.

Advantages for Buyers:

  • Low initial cost, as the core product is free to use and modify.

  • Flexibility to adopt additional premium features as needs grow.

  • Reduced dependencies since the open-core remains accessible even if the commercial relationship ends.

Challenges:

  • Key functionalities may require payment.

  • Some dependency especially for hardware that needs to be manufactured by a company with the right expertise.

SaaS / Managed Hosting

With Software as-a-Service, suppliers can offer cloud-hosted, managed versions of open-source software. This facilitates rapid deployment.

Advantages for Buyers:

  • Operational simplicity, as suppliers handle infrastructure, updates, and security.

  • Predictable pricing via subscriptions, often with tiered support levels.

  • Enterprise reliability, including SLAs for uptime and performance.

Challenges:

  • Supplier dependent, making migrations or customization difficult.

  • Ongoing costs, which can exceed self-hosted deployments over time.

Professional Support

Here, the technology is fully open, but suppliers provide consulting, training, or integration services. This can be relevant for complex critical systems

Advantages for Buyers:

  • Expert assistance for integration, troubleshooting, optimization, and compliance.

  • No licensing fees, paying only for required services.

  • Long-term stability, with vendors ensuring updates and security patches.

Challenges:

  • Can be costly.

  • In-house expertise can still be needed for day-to-day operations.

blocks.body_html:
We’ve just explored three of the most common commercial approaches to open-source technologies. Each has clear strengths, but also trade-offs that procurement teams need to weigh carefully.

To make the differences easier to see, here’s a side-by-side comparison that highlights when each model works best, its main advantage, and the primary risk to watch out for.

blocks.body_html:
To truly benefit from open technologies, companies need to master the Open Technology Game.

In this lesson, we'll look at a structured framework that guides organizations through the five progressive levels of engagement with open technology ecosystems.

Adopting Leveraging existing open technologies to reduce costs and accelerate innovation. Contributing Becoming a visible participant to access open technology ecosystem benefits and signal legitimacy. Steering Shaping the direction of projects and ecosystems to align with strategic goals. Mobilizing Using open technologies tactically to weaken competitors and influence user communities. Projecting Extending open technology influence across multiple domains to reshape industries and infrastructures. 1 2 3 4 5
Sources: MIS Quarterly Executive and The Oxford Handbook of Open Innovation

blocks.complete_hint: Complete the content above before moving on.

blocks.heading_html: Level 1: Adopting – Tapping into open technologies
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

At the initial level of engagement, organizations begin their journey into the open technology ecosystem by adopting existing open technologies. This primarily involves leveraging mature, community-supported Open technologies to reduce costs, accelerate development cycles, and increase flexibility.

Strategic Rationale
In a context of increasing technological change, open technologies offer modularity, reuse, and access to global innovation. They allow firms to avoid dependency risks with proprietary suppliers and foster faster integration of cutting-edge capabilities.

Implementation Actions
To adopt effectively, organizations must:

items_html: Secure legal and compliance support as legal clarity is non-negotiable.
Develop internal integration capabilities or work with trusted partners who can assist with the implementation, customization, and lifecycle support of open technologies.
Educate leadership on the strategic role of open technologies, focusing on licensing, community governance models, and benefits.

blocks.body_html: However, adoption without a minimum of internal capability development can be dead-end. Companies need to have a minimum set of required capabilities to benefit from the autonomy and agility that open technologies are meant to confer.

blocks.heading_html: Level 2: Contributing – Becoming a visible contributor to open technologies
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

As firms move beyond consumption, they begin to contribute back to the Open technology ecosystems they rely on. Contribution signals commitment, competence, and alignment with community values. This transition is typically accompanied by cultural and structural changes within the organization.

Strategic Rationale
Contribution strengthens the firm’s reputation as a technology player and improves its access to knowledge. It also attracts high-calibre developers who seek meaningful engagement and visibility. Furthermore, contributing enhances innovation capacity by ensuring that internal development is compatible with, and responsive to, the evolution of external open technologies

Implementation Actions
To embed contribution into the organizational fabric:

items_html: Establish a Program Office to formalize participation and oversee compliance, strategy, and reporting.
Enable developer autonomy, allowing them to contribute meaningfully and visibly to upstream projects.
Select projects strategically, aligning contributions with future strategic domains or critical dependencies.
Foster an Open technology-oriented culture, educating managers, legal teams, and product owners about the value of collaborative innovation.

blocks.body_html: This level challenges conventional intellectual property paradigms and traditional models of R&D secrecy. Contributions to open technologies often face internal scepticism rooted in risk-aversion and control logics. Overcoming these barriers requires a deliberate change management programme, including storytelling, executive buy-in, and cross-functional engagement.

blocks.heading_html: Level 3: Steering – Shaping open technology projects
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Having established legitimacy through contribution, organizations can now begin to steer the trajectory of specific open technology projects they engage with. This level is about influence over project roadmaps, governance mechanisms, and community norms.

Strategic Rationale
Steering provides access to decision-making circles and early signals about future directions. It allows firms to align the development of key technologies with their own strategic agenda, while reinforcing their position as thought leaders in the ecosystem.

Implementation Actions
To acquire influence, firms can:

items_html: Assume formal roles in project governance, such as maintainers, technical steering committee members, or board representatives.
Support contributor pipelines, through mentorship, funding, or organizational sponsorship of maintainers and developers.

blocks.body_html: At this level, reputation becomes currency. Those who consistently act as responsible community stewards enjoy higher influence and trust. The firm’s ability to shape both technical and normative aspects of open technology ecosystems becomes a strategic advantage.

blocks.heading_html: Level 4: Mobilizing – Using open technologies to undermine the competition
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

With steering capabilities in place, firms can escalate their game by using open technologies as a strategic lever to reshape competitive landscapes. This involves more assertive and sometimes adversarial moves.

Strategic Rationale
Openness is not only a method of collaboration, it can also be a competitive weapon. Firms at this level use open technologies to commoditise competitors’ proprietary offerings, redirect user bases, and establish de facto standards that shift control away from incumbents.

Implementation Actions
Mobilization may include:

items_html: Targeting adjacent domains: Introducing open technology alternatives where competitors rely on closed infrastructures.
Releasing internal technologies to destabilise proprietary markets and attract new users and contributors.

blocks.body_html: To play successfully at this level, senior executives must relinquish short-term control to gain long-term dominance. The paradox is that giving away certain assets, under the right conditions can erode competitors’ advantages more effectively than head-to-head proprietary battles.

blocks.heading_html: Level 5: Projecting – Building the future with open technologies
blocks.body_html: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

At the highest level of the game, firms become architects of future infrastructures. They move beyond projects or domains to shape multi-layered ecosystems, using open technologies as a vehicle for ecosystem orchestration and industry transformation.

Strategic Rationale
By extending openness across layers – software, hardware, data, and standards – firms can eliminate bottlenecks, accelerate adoption, and position themselves as indispensable actors in the value creation architecture of tomorrow’s industries.

Implementation Actions
To project at scale:

items_html: Operate across multiple layers of the stack.
Launch new initiatives in underdeveloped or strategically important domains.
Synchronise openness with proprietary complements, ensuring that the open technologies foster environments where the firm’s differentiated assets thrive.

blocks.body_html: An example of this is Google’s AI initiatives. The company released Its AI framework to catalyse community adoption of its machine learning tools. It also opened large datasets to accelerate AI research and published key papers on AI technologies. At the same time, it integrated AI in its product and services to generate value out of it.

blocks.body_html:
The open technology game is not just about technology – it’s about strategy, culture, and leadership.

Firms that treat open technologies as a procurement choice will capture cost savings. Firms that treat them as a strategic game can capture influence, legitimacy, and long-term advantage.

Mastering the game means asking:

items_html: Where are we today?
What level do we want to reach?
Do we have the capabilities and mindset to get there?

blocks.body_html: The firms that can answer these questions confidently will not only thrive in today’s digital landscape but also shape the infrastructures and industries of tomorrow.

blocks.body_html: You’ve now explored the essential knowledge and skills for procuring open technologies, including OCP-based hardware and open-source solutions. Let's recap the key takeaways.

items_html:
What Are Open Technologies?
Openness isn’t about price – it’s about freedom. Open technologies grant the rights to use, study, modify, and share solutions. These principles now extend across software, hardware, data, and standards, powering much of today’s digital world.

Open-Source Licenses
Licenses are the legal backbone of open ecosystems. They define how technology can be used and shared. Procurement professionals must understand the distinctions between copyleft (contaminating and non-contaminating) and permissive licenses, as these determine compliance obligations, risks, and opportunities.

Qualifying an Open Ecosystem
Unlike traditional procurement, working with open technologies means qualifying ecosystems, not just suppliers. Seven criteria – cost optimisation, design flexibility, stability, transparency, supplier flexibility, licensing, and ecosystem vibrancy – help teams assess fitness for purpose and long-term viability.

Open-Source Commercial Models
Adopting open technologies requires aligning with the right business model. Three common approaches include:

  • Open-Core (low-cost entry with optional premium features),

  • SaaS/Managed Hosting (outsourced ease, but vendor-dependent),

  • Professional Support (expert services for complex systems).

Each offers trade-offs in cost, control, and scalability.

Mastering the Open Technology Game
Engagement with open ecosystems follows five progressive levels: Adopting, Contributing, Steering, Mobilising, and Projecting. Each level requires new capabilities and strategic choices – from reducing costs and gaining visibility, to shaping industry-wide ecosystems and influencing the future of technology.

blocks.body_html: Open technologies are no longer a niche option – they are the foundation of modern digital infrastructures. By mastering this knowledge, you can make informed procurement decisions, collaborate effectively with open technology communities, and leverage OCP-based and open-source products to drive innovation and strategic advantage.
